description: We are a team of students from the Polytechnic Lyceum of NTUU "KPI" in Kyiv, united by our passion for programming, modern technology, and new ideas. We enjoy experimenting, creating our own projects, solving interesting challenges, and learning new things. Each of us has different strengths, so we complement and support each other while working together to find creative solutions.
summary:
AstraLink: Mission Operations is a 2D educational space game created by our team, PL KPI, using Unity and C#.
Our main idea was to make learning programming more exciting. We were inspired by Scratch, but instead of controlling characters, players build and program their own spacecraft.
In our game, players choose space mission contracts, select satellite components, and work with limited resources such as budget, mass, power, and communication. The most important part is programming the spacecraft using simple IF–THEN–ELSE rules. Players then launch their missions, explore an interactive solar system, and watch how their decisions affect the satellite in real time.
We also created A.S.T.R.A., our own language model trained from scratch, which explains mission results, gives advice, and even makes jokes.
Our game addresses the NASA challenge by combining spacecraft design, resource management, and autonomous control.
We believe that learning through experiments, mistakes, and discoveries is much more interesting than simply reading about programming or space.
details:
We are Team PL KPI, a group of six students who love programming, technology, and space. When we started this challenge, we wanted to create something that would be both fun and educational.

We were inspired by Scratch, where beginners can learn programming by controlling characters. But we had another idea: what if you could program a spacecraft instead? What if your code could save a satellite from running out of power or help it survive a solar storm?

That's how AstraLink: Mission Operations was born.

How our game works

In AstraLink, players become space mission engineers. They choose a mission, build their spacecraft, and prepare it for launch.

Players have to manage six important resources: budget, mass, power, data, communication, and reliability. They can choose different rockets, batteries, solar panels, antennas, and scientific instruments. Every decision matters because there are no unlimited resources in space.

But the most interesting part begins when players program their spacecraft.

Using simple IF–THEN–ELSE rules, they can create their own autopilot. For example, if the battery level becomes too low, the satellite can automatically turn off scientific instruments to save energy. If radiation becomes dangerous, it can switch to Safe Mode.

After launch, players can follow their spacecraft on an interactive Solar System Map. They can watch its movement, monitor telemetry, and see which programmed rules are being executed.

Sometimes the mission succeeds. Sometimes something goes wrong. And that's exactly what makes the game educational.

Core mechanics

- Contract Hub & R&D Tech Tree: Players choose contracts across LEO, Lunar, and Mars orbits, manage agency capital and passive income, and unlock new hardware tiers and autopilot CPU slots in an interactive, zoomable tech tree.

- Spacecraft Hangar: Players build their spacecraft from scratch by selecting a rocket, spacecraft bus, solar panels or RTG, battery, antenna with SSD storage, and science payload while balancing budget, mass, power, data, communication, and reliability.

- Block-Based Autopilot Programming: Players program onboard autonomy from scratch using visual IF–THEN–ELSE rule blocks—reacting to battery level, solar power, radiation, and communication windows without writing text code.

- Solar System Mission Map: Players track their spacecraft in real time around Earth, the Moon, and Mars using a zoomable and draggable map with live telemetry charts, sunlight/eclipse indicators, delayed manual commands, and active autopilot rule highlights.

- Post-Flight Debrief: After every flight, players inspect key telemetry metrics, score breakdowns, and root-cause diagnostics, with free retries to refine their build and code.

Meet A.S.T.R.A. — our own AI assistant

We didn't want players to see only a simple "Mission Failed" message. We wanted them to understand what happened and learn from their mistakes.

That's why we created A.S.T.R.A., our own small AI assistant. We trained its model from scratch using data prepared by our team. It analyzes mission results, identifies different situations, and selects suitable explanations, advice, or funny comments from a collection of prepared responses.

A.S.T.R.A. doesn't write completely new answers like a large language model. Instead, it helps players understand their decisions using the information we taught it.

How we developed the game

We developed AstraLink using Unity 2D and C#. Our team independently created the game concept, story, mission mechanics, and the core physics and simulation logic.

We also used Google Antigravity with Gemini models to help us write, improve, and debug other parts of the game. These tools helped us work faster, but we reviewed the results, tested the features, and made the final development decisions ourselves.

For graphics, music, and sound effects, we used licensed asset packs. We built the game for WebGL so that players can launch it directly in their browsers through itch.io, without installing additional software.

How NASA science helped us

We wanted our space missions to be based on real scientific ideas.

We used NASA information about solar energy, communication delays between planets, and solar storms. These concepts helped us design situations where players must think carefully about spacecraft resources and automatic decisions.

Of course, we simplified some real-world processes. For example, communication between Earth and Mars can take several minutes, but in our game the delay is shortened to 10 seconds so players can experience its effects without waiting too long.

We tried to find a balance between scientific accuracy, educational value, and enjoyable gameplay.

Why we believe AstraLink matters

We believe programming becomes much more interesting when you can see what your algorithms actually do.

In AstraLink, players don't just learn IF–THEN–ELSE statements. They use them to solve problems, make engineering decisions, and explore space.

Our goal is to show students that making mistakes is a normal part of learning. If a spacecraft fails, they can change their algorithm, try again, and discover a better solution.

And maybe, after playing AstraLink, someone will become interested in programming, engineering, or even working on real space missions in the future.

For us, that would be the biggest success of this project.
